prize_parts.citation: for evidence on how import competition and technological change reshape local labour markets, employment and wages

statement.case_for: The China-shock research of Autor, Dorn and Hanson is among the clearest examples of the credibility tradition applied to a first-order question. It measures how exposure to import competition shapes employment, wages, transfers and mobility across local labour markets. The designs are transparent enough to be criticised, replicated and extended, and that has happened. The work changed both research agendas and policy debate on trade adjustment, and it set a template for local-labour-market studies well beyond trade. More than a decade has passed since the core papers, which is enough time for persistence and adjustment work to refine the original findings. After the opening round, my view is that this three-name group offers the tightest attribution of any shortlisted entry that I rank highly.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is identification and interpretation. The shift-share exposure measures and instruments have been debated, and the long-run size and persistence of the effects are not settled. The ballot entry also bundles two distinct strands, the task and skill-bias literature and the trade-shock literature. The preferred trio credits only the second strand in full and leaves Katz, whose skill-premium work is foundational, outside the citation. Lineages outside the credited names, including the task-framework contributions of an earlier laureate, complicate any claim that the technology half is fully recognised.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B036 first with Autor, Katz and Hanson. She attributes the task and skill-bias line mainly to Katz and Autor, and the trade-exposure line to Autor and Hanson with Dorn as an important co-author. She notes that omitting Dorn is a real cost.
responses.response: I agree that Dorn's omission would be costly, and that is why I would credit him rather than Katz. A citation naming Katz needs to cover the skill-premium and education-technology strand, which is a separate and older discovery with its own lineage. The three-name cap then forces a choice between one coherent finding and a looser bundle. I would sooner credit the empirical programme that Autor, Dorn and Hanson wrote jointly. I accept that this leaves Katz's contribution unrecognised, and I do not think the Committee should pretend otherwise.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B036 second with Autor, Hanson and Dorn. He observes that the task-based and trade-shock contributions are distinct and may be hard to bundle, and that Katz's core contribution sits near work already recognised.
responses.response: I largely agree, and I take the point about bundling as an argument for a narrow citation. I would add one qualification. A narrow citation makes the prize a statement about trade and local labour markets. It should not be read as a verdict on the technology strand. The Committee should state this scope openly in the citation, so that the choice is not mistaken for a ruling on the origins of the task framework. Where I differ from Teorell is in giving more weight to how mature and identifiable the trade-shock evidence is than to the broader technology narrative.

responses.point: Stromberg ranks B036 sixth and proposes Autor and Katz. He anchors the case in the task framework and skill-biased technical change. He notes that Dorn and Hanson are central to the China-shock empirics and that Acemoglu, who shares the task framework, is absent from the credited set.
responses.response: I disagree with the pairing of Autor and Katz as the core, although Stromberg's reasoning about Acemoglu is a fair warning. The task framework has the most diffuse attribution on this ballot. Credit there is shared with people who are not credited and with a recipient who has already been honoured, so the attribution problem is hardest on exactly that strand. The trade-shock empirics have a sharper attribution to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Dropping Hanson and Dorn would strip the citation of the evidence that has had the largest effect on policy debate, so I would not take that route.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B036 seventh. He acknowledges the strong policy relevance but doubts whether the maturity bar is met. He cites ongoing debate on identification, persistence and the magnitude of the China shock, and the overlap with Acemoglu's recognised work on technology and tasks.
responses.response: I take the identification point seriously. It is the right question to ask of this kind of evidence, and the 2021 speech's emphasis on what exactly a natural experiment identifies applies here too. I do not think the debate counts against maturity. The disagreement concerns magnitudes and long-run persistence. The finding that import exposure lowered local employment and wages is robust to the main critiques, and the follow-up work on adjustment has refined it. Prizes have regularly recognised work whose size estimates remained contested while the central discovery was established. The task-framework overlap is real, which is why I prefer the trade-shock citation to a combined technology-and-trade citation.

uncertainties: How far shift-share exposure measures and instruments support the long-run magnitude and persistence claims for the China shock.

Whether the Committee should read the entry as a trade-shock prize or insist on a broader technology-and-tasks prize that would bring Katz in and raise the attribution problem with the earlier laureate.
Whether the recent labour, technology and institutions prizes leave room for another award on the labour-market effects of trade and technology.
Whether authors outside the credited names have strong enough claims to the empirical programme to change the attribution.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. Fredriksson has no listed co-authorship or institutional tie to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz. His field proximity to empirical labour economics and quasi-experimental policy evaluation is disclosed, and it may make him more receptive to design-based work.
